title: How a guest instruction runs on KVM
summary: Most instructions run directly on the CPU; a few leave the guest.

steps.n: Ordinary instructions in the guest, such as arithmetic, run on the real CPU at full speed.
The guest tries something only a kernel may do, such as touching a hardware register.
The CPU stops the guest and hands control to the KVM module in the host kernel (a VM exit).
KVM deals with simple causes itself, such as a timer or a page fault, and resumes the guest.
If the guest touched a virtual device such as a disk controller, KVM passes the request to QEMU.
QEMU emulates the device, KVM re-enters the guest and it continues as if real hardware answered.

title: Steal time on an oversubscribed host
summary: Why a guest feels slow although its own load is low.

steps.n: The guest wants to run a thread and its virtual CPU becomes ready.
Many other guests on the same cores are also busy, so more vCPUs want time than there are cores.
The host scheduler runs a different guest vCPU first, and the first one waits in the queue.
After a delay the guest vCPU gets a core. The guest sees time pass without its code running.
The guest kernel counts the wait as steal time, shown as st in top and vmstat.
The operator moves a guest to another host or lowers the vCPU to core ratio, and steal time falls.

title: A qcow2 snapshot chain
summary: How writes after a snapshot go to a new layer.

steps.n: The admin takes a snapshot. The current disk image becomes read-only.
A new overlay file is created that records only the blocks that change from now on.
All new writes from the guest go to the overlay, so the base image stays untouched.
A read looks in the overlay and falls back to the base image for blocks never changed.
The longer the guest runs, the more blocks the overlay holds, and a chain of overlays slows reads.
The admin merges the overlay back with a block commit or deletes the snapshot, which frees the space.

title: Traffic through a Linux bridge
summary: From guest to physical network.

steps.n: The guest virtual NIC writes a frame that appears on a tap device on the host.
The bridge records that the guest MAC address lives behind this tap port.
The bridge checks its table. Unknown or outside addresses go out of the uplink.
The frame is sent to the physical NIC that is attached to the bridge.
The frame reaches the physical switch, which forwards it on its VLAN.
The reply comes back through the same ports and the bridge delivers it to the right tap.

title: A VLAN tag on a trunk
summary: Two networks over one cable.

steps.n: Guest A sends a normal frame. It does not know about VLANs.
The host bridge port for guest A is assigned VLAN 10, so the frame is tagged 10 on the way out.
The same happens for guest B with VLAN 20, over the same uplink.
Both tagged frames leave through the trunk port that carries VLANs 10 and 20.
The switch keeps VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 apart, so A and B cannot reach each other without a router.
On the way back the host removes the tag and delivers the frame to the correct guest.

title: Why a migration does not converge
summary: A busy guest dirties memory faster than the network copies it.

steps.n: The source starts copying every memory page of the guest to the destination.
A busy database writes to memory the whole time, so pages already copied become stale again.
Round two copies only the pages changed in round one, over the same network link.
If the guest dirties pages faster than the link can carry them, each round is as large as the last.
The migration never reaches the small final step, and the operator sees it still running after minutes.
The admin enables auto-converge to slow the guest or compression, and the final switch can finish.

title: HA restarts guests after a host dies
summary: What a cluster does when a host fails.

steps.n: The cluster manager stops receiving heartbeats from the host.
After a timeout it marks the host as suspect, since a network cut would look the same.
It cuts power to the host through a fencing device, so the old guests cannot still be writing to the disks.
The fencing device reports success, which is the only safe signal that the guests are really stopped.
The manager restarts the guests on surviving hosts using the shared storage.
Each guest boots again, with a short outage, and the operator investigates the dead host.

title: Cloning from a template
summary: How a new guest starts from a golden image.

steps.n: The admin builds a clean guest, removes machine-specific data and keeps it as a read-only template.
A new overlay is created that uses the template as its backing file, which takes seconds.
The new guest boots from the overlay and reads unchanged blocks from the template.
cloud-init sets the hostname, keys and network, so the clone becomes a distinct machine.
All changes go to the clone overlay, so the template is never modified by guests.
A patched template is built later and new clones use it, while old ones keep their old base.

title: Failure and recovery: the pool fills and guests pause
summary: Old snapshots consume the storage pool.

steps.n: Snapshots taken weeks ago keep growing as guests write, and nobody reviews them.
Free space shrinks until the pool has almost nothing left for new writes.
A guest tries to write a new block, the host cannot allocate space, and the guest is paused with an I/O error.
Monitoring alerts only on the guest pause, because pool usage had no threshold alert.
The operator lists snapshots per guest with the hypervisor tools and finds two old ones.
Using the proper command merges or drops the chain safely, and the pool gains free space.
Guests are resumed, and the team adds pool usage alerts and a snapshot expiry policy.

title: A write through the page cache
summary: Why data is not on disk when write returns.

steps.n: The application writes data and the kernel stores it in the page cache in memory, then returns.
The pages are marked dirty and wait for a later flush, so a power cut now would lose them.
A careful program calls fsync to demand that the data and metadata reach stable storage.
The filesystem writes the intent to its journal so a crash can be recovered consistently.
The journal and data blocks are written to the device, which may have its own cache.
Only now does the call return, so the application knows the data should survive a power loss.

title: What happens at boot when fstab is wrong
summary: A bad line in /etc/fstab and a stuck boot.

steps.n: At boot systemd reads /etc/fstab and creates a mount unit for each line.
One line names a device by /dev/sdb1, but after a hardware change the name has moved.
systemd waits for the device until a timeout of about ninety seconds and then marks the mount failed.
Services that need that mount are skipped and the system drops into emergency mode.
The operator edits the line to use UUID=... from blkid, and adds nofail for non-critical mounts.
mount -a succeeds without errors, and the machine starts normally after a reboot.

title: Growing a logical volume online
summary: Add space to a mounted filesystem without downtime.

steps.n: vgs shows free space in the volume group. If none, a new disk must be added to the group first.
lvextend -L +20G adds twenty gigabytes of extents to the logical volume.
The block device is bigger now, but the filesystem on it still thinks it has the old size.
resize2fs for ext4 or xfs_growfs for XFS expands the filesystem while it stays mounted.
df -h now shows the extra capacity and applications keep running throughout.
The admin notes the new size and checks that the volume group still has headroom.

title: Writing to RAID 5 and the write penalty
summary: Why small writes cost four I/Os.

steps.n: The application changes one block in the array.
The controller must first read the old data block from its disk.
It also reads the old parity block for that stripe.
New parity is old parity XOR old data XOR new data, calculated in memory.
The new data block is written to the data disk.
The new parity block is written, giving four I/Os for one logical write, which is the write penalty.

title: An NFS mount and a read
summary: From open to bytes.

steps.n: The application opens a file under /mnt/shared as if it were local.
The NFS client sends a request to the server asking for the file handle of that name.
The server checks the export rules and the file permissions for the caller.
The server replies with a file handle that identifies the file on the server.
A read of a range of bytes goes to the server, over TCP, and may be cached on the client.
The bytes arrive and the application sees them. A slow network shows up as slow reads.

title: Ceph places an object
summary: No central lookup table.

steps.n: The client hashes the object name to a placement group and uses CRUSH to find which OSDs hold it.
No central server is asked. The client talks directly to the primary OSD for that group.
The primary sends the write to the replica OSDs on other hosts, as the failure domain rules require.
Each replica confirms that the data is safely stored.
Only after all replicas respond does the primary tell the client the write is complete.
If an OSD dies, CRUSH recomputes placement and the cluster copies data to restore the replica count.

title: df says full but du disagrees
summary: A deleted file that is still open.

steps.n: df -h shows the volume at 100 percent used.
du -sh finds only a fraction of that space in visible files.
The gap means space is held by something that is not in any directory.
lsof +L1 shows a log file that was deleted while a process still has it open.
The kernel cannot free the blocks until the last process closes the file descriptor.
Restarting the process, or truncating through /proc, releases the space and df drops.

title: A backup you can restore
summary: The restore test is part of the backup.

steps.n: The scheduler starts the backup job at night when load is low.
The job copies data to the backup store and checks the size and checksums.
The job sends a result with size and duration, and an alert fires if it is missing.
Once a week another job restores a sample into a scratch system.
The test opens the restored database or files and compares counts with the source.
A failed restore raises an alert, so a backup that cannot be restored is found early.

title: Failure and recovery: out of inodes
summary: Creating files fails although space is free.

steps.n: A service writes one tiny file per request into a single directory.
The filesystem has free blocks but every inode is used, so it cannot describe a new file.
The application sees no space left on device errors while df -h shows 40 percent free.
Errors reach monitoring, but disk usage looks fine, which confuses the first responder.
df -i shows 100 percent of inodes used, which explains the failure.
The operator removes expired files in batches and finds the directory that holds millions of them.
The team adds inode alerts, changes the app to a directory tree or object storage, and sizes inodes at mkfs.

title: How the planner picks a plan
summary: From SQL text to a chosen strategy.

steps.n: The client sends SQL. The parser checks the syntax and builds a tree of the request.
The planner receives the tree and lists possible ways to run it, such as index scan or full scan.
It reads table statistics for row counts and value distributions to estimate the cost of each way.
The plan with the lowest estimated cost wins, even if the estimate is wrong.
The executor runs it step by step and returns rows to the client.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows both. A big gap points to stale statistics.

title: An index lookup versus a scan
summary: Why the same query takes 4 ms or 4 seconds.

steps.n: The query asks for the orders of one customer from a table of fifty million rows.
Without an index the planner must read every row of the table and test each one.
With an index on customer_id the planner descends a small tree to the matching entries.
Only the few rows found are fetched from the table.
A handful of reads returns in milliseconds, instead of reading the whole table.
Every insert and update must also update the index, which is why unneeded indexes hurt.

title: A deadlock between two transactions
summary: Each waits for a lock held by the other.

steps.n: Transaction A updates row 1 and holds a lock on it.
Transaction B updates row 2 and holds a lock on it.
Transaction A now tries to update row 2 and waits for B.
Transaction B tries to update row 1 and waits for A, so neither can continue.
After a short timeout the database finds the cycle of waits.
It aborts one transaction with a deadlock error, the other proceeds, and the application retries the failed one.

title: A pooler in front of the database
summary: Many clients, few server connections.

steps.n: Each app instance opens many connections, far more than the database should hold.
The pooler keeps a small number of server connections and hands them out per transaction.
The database sees twenty active connections instead of five hundred.
Results flow back through the pooler to the right client.
When all server connections are busy, new requests wait briefly rather than overloading the database.
Monitoring tracks waiting clients and pool usage, a sign of capacity limits.

title: Replication lag builds up
summary: A replica falls behind the primary.

steps.n: Every change is written to the write-ahead log and streamed to the replica.
The replica applies the log records in order to stay current.
A long reporting query on the replica holds old row versions that replay must wait for.
New log records arrive faster than they are applied, and lag grows to minutes.
The application reads stale values from the replica and users report missing changes.
Moving heavy reports elsewhere or tuning conflict settings lets replay catch up and lag fall.

title: Vacuum reclaims dead rows
summary: Updates leave old versions behind.

steps.l: UPDATE creates a new row version
steps.n: PostgreSQL writes a new version and keeps the old one for transactions that may still need it.
Once no transaction needs the old versions they are dead but still take space.
When dead rows pass a threshold, autovacuum scans the table and marks that space reusable.
It also refreshes statistics so the planner makes good choices.
New rows fit into the freed space and the table stops growing.
An old open transaction prevents cleanup, so bloat grows even when vacuum runs.

title: Adding an index without blocking writes
summary: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY step by step.

steps.n: The operator runs CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which does not take a lock that blocks writes.
The database scans the table once and builds the index while writers continue.
Inserts and updates run normally, and their changes are recorded for the next pass.
A second pass adds the changes made during the first scan.
The build waits for transactions that started before it, then marks the index valid.
The operator checks the index is valid and confirms the plan now uses it.

title: Failure and recovery: connections exhausted
summary: Every afternoon the API starts failing.

steps.n: At 15:00 traffic rises and each pod opens more connections to handle it.
The database reaches max_connections and refuses new ones with a reserved-slots error.
The API returns errors, and retries open even more connections, making it worse.
Monitoring shows errors and a database connection count at its limit.
pg_stat_activity shows most connections idle in transaction from one service.

steps.l: Add a pooler and fix the leak
steps.n: A pooler caps server connections and the service is fixed to close transactions promptly.
The team alerts on connection usage at 80 percent so the next rise is seen before errors.

title: One LLM request through a serving stack
summary: From prompt to streamed tokens.

steps.n: The client sends a prompt and starts waiting for a streaming response.
The server tokenises the prompt and adds it to the scheduler queue.
The GPU processes all prompt tokens in parallel and builds the key and value tensors.
Those tensors are kept in GPU memory so later tokens need not recompute them.
Each step generates one token using the cache and streams it to the client.

steps.l: Free the cache at the end
steps.n: When the answer finishes, the cache memory is released for other requests.

title: Continuous batching
summary: New requests join a running batch.

steps.n: Request A is generating tokens as part of the current batch.
Request B arrives while A is still running.
A static batcher would make B wait until the whole batch finished, wasting time.

steps.l: Add B at the next step
steps.n: Continuous batching adds B to the batch at the very next decode step.
When A finishes, its slot is freed at once and a waiting request can use it.
The GPU always has a full batch, so throughput is much higher at similar latency.

title: Scheduling a pod onto a GPU
summary: From a resource request to a running container.

steps.n: The pod asks for one GPU in its resource limits.
The device plugin on each GPU node reports how many GPUs it has to the kubelet.
The scheduler picks a node with a free GPU and all other requirements met.
The kubelet asks the device plugin to allocate a specific GPU for the pod.
The container runtime exposes the GPU device and driver libraries inside the container.
nvidia-smi inside the container lists the GPU, and the model can load.

title: Tensor parallelism across GPUs
summary: One model split over two cards.

steps.l: Model too big for one card
steps.n: The weights do not fit in the memory of a single GPU.
Every layer is divided, so GPU 0 and GPU 1 each hold half of its weights.
Both GPUs compute their half of the layer at the same time on the same input.
They combine the halves with an all-reduce over the interconnect after each layer.
On a slow link the exchange dominates, which is why NVLink is preferred inside one node.
After the last layer a token is produced, with some cost in communication for the benefit of fitting the model.

title: Scaling on queue depth
summary: Why CPU is the wrong signal for a GPU service.

steps.n: More requests arrive and replicas start to queue them.
The GPU shows high use even at modest load, so it tells little about spare capacity.
The number of waiting requests and the time to first token increase.
The autoscaler uses queue depth or latency as its scaling signal.
A new replica is scheduled, but loading a model can take minutes.
Once the new replica is ready the queue drains, and warm spare capacity avoids the delay next time.

title: Quantisation to fit a model
summary: Trading precision for memory.

steps.n: A 70-billion parameter model needs about 140 GB at 16 bits, more than one card holds.
The quantiser stores weights in 8 or 4 bits, shrinking the memory by two to four times.

steps.l: Fits with room for the cache
steps.n: The smaller weights leave GPU memory for the KV cache and more concurrent requests.
The team runs evaluation prompts and compares answers with the full-precision model.
If quality loss is acceptable, the quantised model is used, otherwise a milder format is chosen.
Smaller weights also mean less memory traffic, so tokens per second often rise.

title: A cold start of a model replica
summary: Why a new pod takes minutes to serve.

steps.n: The scheduler places the pod on a node with a free GPU.
The node pulls a container image of several gigabytes, which is slow the first time.
The server downloads tens of gigabytes of model weights from storage.
The weights are copied into GPU memory and the server compiles its kernels.
Only now does the pod report ready and receive traffic.
Baking weights into a cache volume or a node-local disk shortens the next start.

title: Reading GPU health signals
summary: What the metrics say about a slow service.

steps.n: The operator looks at utilisation, memory use, temperature and clocks.
Memory use sits at 98 percent, so the KV cache has no room for more requests.
The clock speed has dropped because of temperature, which lowers throughput.
The logs show requests waiting in the queue and some preempted for lack of cache space.
Lower the maximum context length, add a replica or cool the node, depending on the signal.
Latency and queue length drop, and the memory graph leaves a safe margin.

title: Failure and recovery: CUDA out of memory
summary: A model server crashes on a long prompt.

steps.n: A user sends a prompt with a very long context.
The cache for that request grows with the context and competes with other requests for memory.
The GPU raises a CUDA out of memory error and the process dies.
Monitoring shows the pod restarting and requests failing with 503.
The operator compares the weights, cache size and max context against the card memory.
The server is configured with a smaller max context and a GPU memory utilisation cap below 100 percent.
The team adds memory headroom alerts and a request limit, so one long prompt cannot take the service down.

title: Booting a server in OpenStack
summary: From API call to ACTIVE.

steps.n: The user asks for a server with an image, a flavor and a network. The token is checked first.
The scheduler asks Placement which hosts have enough CPU, memory and disk and picks one.
A message over the queue tells the chosen node to build the instance.
The node asks Neutron for a port and Cinder for any volume, then downloads the image.
Nova calls libvirt, which starts the virtual machine with the requested resources.
The server reports ACTIVE. If any step fails, it shows ERROR with a fault message.

title: Authenticating with Keystone
summary: Getting and using a token.

steps.n: The client sends user, password, domain and project to Keystone.
Keystone validates the credentials and the role assignment on the project.
A scoped token and the service catalog with endpoint addresses come back.
The client calls the Nova endpoint and presents the token in a header.
Nova (through middleware) asks Keystone whether the token is valid and for which project and roles.
The policy decides whether those roles may perform the action, then Nova carries it out.

title: Traffic to a floating IP
summary: Following an SSH connection.

steps.n: The client opens an SSH connection to the public floating IP address.
The Neutron router maps the floating IP to the private address of the server.
The packet is checked against the security group rules attached to the port.
If no rule allows port 22 from the client, the packet is silently dropped and SSH times out.
With a matching rule the packet reaches the server and sshd answers.
Stateful tracking lets the reply go back through the router with the floating IP as its source.

title: A quota stops a request
summary: The request is refused before any host is chosen.

steps.n: The user creates a server needing 8 cores.
Nova counts the project usage, 16 of 20 cores, and adds the new request.
The total of 24 is above 20, so the check fails.
The user gets a quota exceeded error that is a rule, not a fault.
The user either deletes unused servers or asks an admin for a higher limit.
The admin raises the cores limit for the project and the request can succeed.

title: A rolling upgrade
summary: Controller by controller.

steps.n: The operator reads the notes for the upgrade path and database migrations.
A full backup is taken and tested, because migrations cannot always be reversed.
The services on controller 1 are upgraded and the database schema is migrated.
Controller 2 keeps serving API calls with the older code during the change.
Compute agents are upgraded a few at a time, with checks that guests keep running.
Service lists, test servers and logs confirm that every component runs the new version.

title: Attaching a Cinder volume
summary: Block storage to a running server.

steps.n: The user asks Cinder for a 100 GB volume, and the backend (such as Ceph) allocates it.
The user asks Nova to attach the volume to a running server.
Nova asks Cinder how to reach the volume, for example the Ceph pool and image.
The node connects to the backend and presents the volume to libvirt.
A block device such as /dev/vdb appears inside the server.
The user creates a filesystem and mounts it, and the data now lives on the volume, not the server disk.

title: Evacuating a failed compute node
summary: Moving servers off a dead host.

steps.n: Monitoring shows nova-compute down on one node and its servers unreachable.
The operator checks the service list and the BMC, and powers the node off to avoid two copies running.
nova evacuate rebuilds each server on another host using shared storage or the same image.
Healthy nodes start the servers, which keep their addresses and volumes.
The failed node is repaired or replaced before returning to service.
nova-compute is enabled on the repaired node and scheduling resumes.

title: Image caching on compute nodes
summary: Why the second boot is faster.

steps.n: The node asks Glance for the image because it has no local copy.
Glance streams the image over the network, which takes time for a large image.
Nova keeps the base image in a local cache directory on the node.
The instance disk is a copy or an overlay on top of the cached base image.
A later boot of the same image finds it in the cache and starts much faster.
Unused cached images are removed after a period, so disk space is reclaimed.

title: Failure and recovery: No valid host was found
summary: A server goes to ERROR at scheduling time.

steps.n: The user requests a flavor with 64 GB of memory.
The scheduler asks for hosts that can fit the request.
Placement returns no candidates, because no node has enough free memory in one piece.
The scheduler gives up and the server goes to ERROR with No valid host was found.
The user reports the failure and the admin reads the fault in server show.
The admin compares free memory per hypervisor and finds the largest block is 48 GB.
The admin adds a node or the user picks a smaller flavor, and the retry succeeds.

title: Finding the slow step in a plan
summary: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE from the inside out.

steps.n: The operator runs EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) so the query really executes and timings are real.
Each node shows actual time and rows; the deepest nodes feed the ones above.
A node that expected 10 rows but returned 2 million shows bad statistics.
A sequential scan on a large table with a filter that removes most rows takes most of the time.
Add an index, rewrite the filter, or run ANALYZE so the planner sees real distributions.
The new plan shows an index scan and a fall in time, which confirms the fix.
